new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (page 5 of, header 'UNCEN-SIL 1/85/5 (DRAFT ONLY) BAHASA: Tefaro'). Below entry 218 the handwritten note reads exactly 'Phonetics: r̆/l̆ interchangeable / a.a = syllable break or ?stop ?? / Stress not reliable'. The only differences from the reader's quote are interpretive: the diacritics on r and l are small hooks/breves in the handwriting, and the symbol before 'stop' is a question-mark-shaped glyph that the reader rendered as glottal stop ʔ (a fair reading, since the note is asking whether 'a.a' is a syllable break or a glottal stop). 'Stress not reliable' is there word for word. The scanned text layer has no hit for stress/phonetic/reliable, so the quote is verifiable only from t…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for Tefaro. This is the only stress-bearing primary data found for the language (the companion Jones 1987 wordlist, already opened in the earlier reading, carries no stress marks). It adds stress-marked forms with a penultimate tendency plus the compilers' own disclaimer 'Stress not reliable'; it neither agrees with nor contradicts anything recorded.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The wordlist does not state a stress rule. The transcription marks primary stress with a raised stroke before the stressed syllable in most multisyllabic entries (e.g. eˈnoha 'ear', oˈmala 'nose', deˈgare 'sun', ˈtoha 'mountain', ˈdama 'person', waˈdoha 'in front', otɔmaˈgahaⁱ 'lie down'; final-marked gaˈdjɛ 'sick', waˈbaⁱ 'sand', bɛˈɛ 'full', deˈdɛ 'stand'; earlier-marked uˈsihɛto 'fly', aˈsimageⁱ 'thunder', ˈatoma 'belly'). By a rough hand tally from the page images the marked syllable is the penult in the large majority of clearly marked multisyllabic forms (order of 95-100), the final syllable in a minority (order of 15, most of them with a superscript off-glide vowel), and an earlier syllable in a few 4-5-syllable forms (order of 10). But the compilers themselves write on p. 5 'Stress not reliable', so the marks cannot support a rule; at most they suggest a penultimate tendency to be confirmed by a real description.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None marked; nothing said. A few forms carry two raised strokes (ˈteˈoge 'swollen', aⁱˈˈdjadoga 'many', weⁱˈwaᵒ 'lightning', aˈˈhute 'spit'), which could be secondary marks or corrections; unreadable as a system.
new_statements.exceptions: No rule and hence no exceptions stated; the note flags r/l interchangeability and uncertainty whether 'a.a' is a syllable break or a glottal stop, which bears on syllable count and hence on where the marks fall.
new_statements.identity_note: The wordlist header reads 'BAHASA: Tefaro (Suku Demba); KAB.: Yapen-Waropen; KEC.: Waren; DESA: Demba; KAMP.: Tefaro; NAMA PENUTUR ASLI: Octofina / Juliana; JENIS KEL.: p/p; UMUR: ±16/16; RELIABILITY: G; AHLI BAHASA: Iris Bouwman / Janny Holster; TANGGAL: 23-5-85' -- i.e. Tefaro as spoken by the Demba people at Tefaro kampung, Demba village, Waren district, elicited from two girls aged about 16. Page 5 adds that the Demba came down from the mountains many years ago fleeing wars and now live at the coast. No other variety is described.

new_statements.citation: one of the works listed for this language (see the second reader's note)
new_statements.check: reported by the second reader, not yet confirmed
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one work is listed for tefa1238 and it was opened with a quotation, so there were no silent or not-opened listed works to spot-check. As a check on the reader's 'conflicts' claim I re-rendered the companion Jones 1987 wordlist (already in the folder from the 09-17 pass; not a listed work, nothing added) and read pp. 1, 4 and 5: the transcription uses ʔ and vowel sequences but no stress strokes at all, the 'Notes on phonetics and transcription' box on p. 4 is blank, and the grammar notes on p. 5 cover word order, tense and person only. Its extracted text layer has no 'stress' hit. So Jones 1987 is genuinely silent on stress; nothing was missed.

sources.note: Nothing. All five pages viewed as images: handwritten phonetic transcription of 200 items (glottal stops, a few length/nasal marks) with no stress marks on any word; the printed box 'Notes on phonetics and transcription' is left blank; 'Existing literature about the language' blank; grammar notes cover only word order, adjective/numeral order, tense adverbs and person. Silent on stress.
